title: Work, Energy and Power
description: Work, Energy and Power — Class 11 Physics (NCERT) notes on work by constant and variable force, work-energy theorem, potential energy, conservation of energy, power and collisions.

topics.title: Work & the Work-Energy Theorem
topics.concept:
Work in physics is not the same as everyday effort. A man holding a heavy suitcase while standing still gets tired, but in the language of physics he does zero work on the suitcase, because it has no displacement. Work is done only when a force succeeds in moving its point of application.

Work done by a constant force. If a constant force $\vec{F}$ acts on a body and the body undergoes a displacement $\vec{s}$, the work done is the scalar (dot) product $W=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}=Fs\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is a scalar; its SI unit is the joule (J), where $1\ \text{J}=1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. The sign of work depends entirely on $\cos\theta$:

  • Positive work ($0\le\theta<90^\circ$): the force has a component along the motion, e.g. gravity on a falling stone.
  • Zero work ($\theta=90^\circ$): the force is perpendicular to motion, e.g. centripetal force on a body in a circle, or the normal reaction on a block sliding horizontally.
  • Negative work ($90^\circ<\theta\le180^\circ$): the force opposes motion, e.g. friction, or gravity on a stone thrown upward.

Work done by a variable force. Most real forces change with position. Over a tiny displacement $dx$ the force is nearly constant, so the small work is $dW=F\,dx$. Adding all such bits gives $W=\int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$. On a force-displacement graph this integral is simply the area under the $F$-$x$ curve. This is the most powerful way to compute work for springs and other position-dependent forces.

Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses because of its motion. For a body of mass $m$ moving with speed $v$, $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$. It is a scalar, always positive, with the same unit (joule) as work. Since momentum $p=mv$, kinetic energy can also be written as $KE=\frac{p^2}{2m}$.

The work-energy theorem ties work and motion together: the net work done by all forces on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, $W_{net}=\Delta KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2-\frac{1}{2}mu^2$. A short derivation for constant acceleration: from $v^2=u^2+2as$ we get $\frac{1}{2}mv^2-\frac{1}{2}mu^2=mas=Fs=W_{net}$. The theorem holds for variable forces too and is often far quicker than using $F=ma$ directly, because it bypasses time and acceleration.

examples.problem: A force of 50 N pulls a box through a displacement of 8 m. The force makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the horizontal direction of motion. Find the work done.
A body of mass 2 kg is lifted vertically upward through 5 m at constant speed. Find (a) the work done by gravity and (b) the work done by the lifting force. Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Weight $=mg=2\times 10=20\ \text{N}$, directed downward; displacement is upward, so $\theta=180^\circ$ for gravity.
  2. Step 2: Work by gravity $=mgs\cos 180^\circ=20\times 5\times(-1)=-100\ \text{J}$.
  3. Step 3: At constant speed the lifting force equals the weight $=20\ \text{N}$ upward, along the motion, so work by lifting force $=20\times 5\times\cos 0^\circ=+100\ \text{J}$.

Answer: (a) $-100\ \text{J}$ by gravity; (b) $+100\ \text{J}$ by the lifting force.

examples.problem: A variable force acting along the x-axis is given by $F=(3x+4)\ \text{N}$, where x is in metres. Find the work done as the body moves from $x=0$ to $x=2\ \text{m}$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For a variable force $W=\int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx=\int_0^2 (3x+4)\,dx$.
  2. Step 2: Integrate: $W=\left[\frac{3x^2}{2}+4x\right]_0^2$.
  3. Step 3: Evaluate: $W=\left(\frac{3\times 4}{2}+8\right)-0=6+8=14\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $W=14\ \text{J}$

examples.problem: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates from rest to 20 m/s. Using the work-energy theorem, find the net work done on the car.
A bullet of mass 20 g moving at 200 m/s strikes a wooden block and is stopped after penetrating 0.1 m. Find the average resistive force offered by the block.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: By the work-energy theorem, work done by the resistive force $=\Delta KE=0-\frac{1}{2}mu^2$.
  2. Step 2: $m=0.02\ \text{kg}$, $u=200\ \text{m/s}$, so $\Delta KE=-\frac{1}{2}\times 0.02\times 200^2=-400\ \text{J}$.
  3. Step 3: The force opposes motion, so $W=-F\times s$, giving $-F\times 0.1=-400$, hence $F=\frac{400}{0.1}=4000\ \text{N}$.

Answer: $F=4000\ \text{N}$

examples.problem: A body moving in a horizontal circle of radius 3 m at constant speed experiences a centripetal force of 12 N. How much work does this force do in one complete revolution?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: The centripetal force always points toward the centre, while the displacement is along the tangent, so the angle between them is $\theta=90^\circ$.
  2. Step 2: Work done $=Fs\cos 90^\circ$, and $\cos 90^\circ=0$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore the work done by the centripetal force is zero (the speed, and hence the kinetic energy, does not change).

Answer: $W=0\ \text{J}$

recap: Work by a constant force is $W=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}=Fs\cos\theta$; it is a scalar measured in joules.
Work is positive, zero or negative depending on whether $\theta$ is acute, $90^\circ$, or obtuse.
For a variable force, $W=\int F\,dx$, which equals the area under the force-displacement graph.
Kinetic energy of a moving body is $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2=\frac{p^2}{2m}$, always positive.
Work-energy theorem: net work done equals change in kinetic energy, $W_{net}=\Delta KE$.

quiz.q: A coolie carries a load on his head and walks on a level platform. The work done by him against gravity on the load is:
quiz.explanation: The displacement is horizontal while gravity (and the supporting force) is vertical, so $\theta=90^\circ$ and $W=Fs\cos 90^\circ=0$.

quiz.q: The work done by a force $\vec{F}=(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j})\ \text{N}$ for a displacement $\vec{s}=(4\hat{i}+\hat{j})\ \text{m}$ is:
If the speed of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
The area under a force-displacement graph represents:
quiz.explanation: Work for a variable force is $W=\int F\,dx$, which is exactly the area under the $F$-$x$ curve.

topics.title: Potential Energy & Conservation
topics.concept:
Potential energy is stored energy a body possesses because of its position or its configuration. A stretched bow, a raised hammer, and a compressed spring all hold energy that can be released to do work later. Unlike kinetic energy, potential energy is always defined relative to a chosen reference level.

Conservative and non-conservative forces. A force is conservative if the work it does on a body depends only on the starting and ending points, not on the path taken, and the work done in a complete round trip is zero. Gravity and the spring force are conservative. Only for conservative forces can we define a potential energy, through $F=-\frac{dU}{dx}$ (force is the negative slope of the potential energy curve). A force is non-conservative if the work depends on the path; friction and air resistance are the standard examples — they convert mechanical energy into heat, so no potential energy can be assigned to them.

Gravitational potential energy. Near the Earth's surface, lifting a body of mass $m$ through a height $h$ requires work $mgh$ against gravity, which is stored as gravitational PE: $U=mgh$, measured from a chosen zero level. This is why a stone at the top of a cliff can do work on the way down.

Spring (elastic) potential energy. A spring obeying Hooke's law exerts a restoring force $F=-kx$, where $k$ is the spring constant (N/m) and $x$ is the extension or compression from the natural length. The work done in stretching it is the area of the triangle under the $F$-$x$ line, giving $U_{spring}=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$. Notice that $U$ depends on $x^2$, so the spring stores the same energy whether stretched or compressed by the same amount.

  • Restoring force grows linearly: $F=-kx$.
  • Stored energy grows as the square: $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$.
  • Doubling the deformation quadruples the stored energy.

Conservation of mechanical energy. When only conservative forces do work, the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of a system stays constant: $KE+PE=\text{constant}$, i.e. $\frac{1}{2}mv^2+U=E$. For a freely falling body, as it descends, PE ($mgh$) steadily converts into KE ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$), so their sum is unchanged. If a non-conservative force such as friction acts, mechanical energy is not conserved — the lost mechanical energy appears as heat, sound or deformation, but the total energy of the universe is still conserved (law of conservation of energy).

examples.problem: A 3 kg block is raised to a height of 8 m above the ground. Find its gravitational potential energy. Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
A spring of force constant 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. Find the potential energy stored in it.
A stone of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m. Using conservation of energy, find its speed just before it hits the ground. Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: By conservation of energy, all the PE at the top converts to KE at the bottom: $mgh=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
  2. Step 2: Mass cancels: $v^2=2gh=2\times 10\times 20=400$.
  3. Step 3: $v=\sqrt{400}=20\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $v=20\ \text{m/s}$

examples.problem: If the extension of a spring is doubled, by what factor does the stored elastic potential energy change?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Spring PE is $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $U\propto x^2$.
  2. Step 2: Replacing $x$ by $2x$ gives $U'=\frac{1}{2}k(2x)^2=\frac{1}{2}k\cdot 4x^2=4\left(\frac{1}{2}kx^2\right)$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $U'=4U$.

Answer: The stored energy becomes 4 times.

examples.problem: A ball of mass 0.2 kg is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 10 m/s. Using conservation of energy, find the maximum height it reaches. Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: At maximum height the ball is momentarily at rest, so all the initial KE becomes PE: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2=mgh$.
  2. Step 2: Mass cancels: $h=\frac{v^2}{2g}=\frac{10^2}{2\times 10}$.
  3. Step 3: $h=\frac{100}{20}=5\ \text{m}$.

Answer: $h=5\ \text{m}$

examples.problem: A 2 kg block slides down a frictionless incline from a height of 5 m. Find its kinetic energy and speed at the bottom. Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: With no friction, mechanical energy is conserved: PE lost = KE gained, so $KE=mgh$.
  2. Step 2: $KE=2\times 10\times 5=100\ \text{J}$.
  3. Step 3: From $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, $v=\sqrt{\frac{2\,KE}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times 100}{2}}=\sqrt{100}=10\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $KE=100\ \text{J}$, $v=10\ \text{m/s}$

recap: A conservative force does path-independent work and zero work over a closed loop; gravity and springs are conservative.
Friction and air resistance are non-conservative; they dissipate mechanical energy as heat.
Gravitational potential energy near the Earth is $U=mgh$, measured from a chosen reference level.
Elastic (spring) potential energy is $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$; the restoring force is $F=-kx$.
When only conservative forces act, total mechanical energy $KE+PE$ stays constant.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non-conservative force?
quiz.explanation: Friction does path-dependent work and dissipates energy as heat, so it is non-conservative.

quiz.q: The potential energy stored in a spring of constant $k$ stretched by $x$ is:
quiz.explanation: The work to stretch a spring is the triangular area under $F=kx$, giving $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$.

quiz.q: A body falls freely from rest. As it falls, its total mechanical energy:
quiz.explanation: With only gravity (a conservative force) acting, $KE+PE$ is conserved; PE simply converts to KE.

quiz.q: The relation between a conservative force and its potential energy is:
quiz.explanation: A conservative force is the negative gradient of potential energy: $F=-\frac{dU}{dx}$.

topics.title: Power & Collisions
topics.concept:
Power measures how fast work is done. Two cranes may lift the same load to the same height — doing identical work — but the one that does it in less time is more powerful. Power is defined as the rate of doing work, $P=\frac{W}{t}$. The SI unit is the watt (W), where $1\ \text{W}=1\ \text{J/s}$. A common practical unit is the horsepower, $1\ \text{hp}=746\ \text{W}$.

Instantaneous power can be written in terms of force and velocity. Since $dW=\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s}$, dividing by $dt$ gives $P=\vec{F}\cdot\frac{d\vec{s}}{dt}=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}=Fv\cos\theta$. This is why a car engine delivering constant power can reach high speed only by reducing its driving force (lower gears give more force at low speed). The kilowatt-hour (kWh) used in electricity billing is a unit of energy, not power: $1\ \text{kWh}=3.6\times 10^6\ \text{J}$.

Collisions are brief interactions in which bodies exert large forces on each other. In every collision, linear momentum is conserved (no net external force during the short impact). Collisions are classified by what happens to kinetic energy:

  • Elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Example: collisions between hard steel balls or gas molecules (ideally).
  • Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not — some is lost to heat, sound or deformation.
  • Perfectly inelastic collision: the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity; the maximum possible kinetic energy is lost (consistent with momentum conservation).

Elastic collision in one dimension. For two bodies $m_1,m_2$ with initial velocities $u_1,u_2$, solving momentum and energy conservation gives the final velocities $v_1=\frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1+2m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ and $v_2=\frac{(m_2-m_1)u_2+2m_1u_1}{m_1+m_2}$. A neat consequence: in a 1D elastic collision the relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation, $u_1-u_2=v_2-v_1$. When equal masses collide elastically and one is at rest, they simply exchange velocities.

Perfectly inelastic collision. If the bodies stick together, momentum conservation gives the common velocity $v=\frac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$.

Coefficient of restitution. Real collisions lie between the two extremes, described by $e=\frac{\text{relative velocity of separation}}{\text{relative velocity of approach}}=\frac{v_2-v_1}{u_1-u_2}$. Here $e=1$ for a perfectly elastic collision, $e=0$ for a perfectly inelastic one, and $0

examples.problem: A pump lifts 600 kg of water through a height of 10 m in 20 s. Find the power of the pump. Take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Work done against gravity $W=mgh=600\times 10\times 10=60000\ \text{J}$.
  2. Step 2: Power $P=\frac{W}{t}=\frac{60000}{20}$.
  3. Step 3: $P=3000\ \text{W}=3\ \text{kW}$.

Answer: $P=3000\ \text{W}=3\ \text{kW}$

examples.problem: A car moves at a constant velocity of 15 m/s while the engine exerts a forward force of 800 N. Find the power developed by the engine.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For force along the velocity, $P=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}=Fv\cos 0^\circ=Fv$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute $F=800\ \text{N}$, $v=15\ \text{m/s}$.
  3. Step 3: $P=800\times 15=12000\ \text{W}=12\ \text{kW}$.

Answer: $P=12000\ \text{W}=12\ \text{kW}$

examples.problem: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary 2 kg ball. Find the velocities of both balls after the collision.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: The masses are equal and the second ball is at rest ($u_1=6\ \text{m/s}$, $u_2=0$, $m_1=m_2$).
  2. Step 2: For equal masses in an elastic collision, the velocities are simply exchanged: $v_1=u_2$ and $v_2=u_1$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $v_1=0$ and $v_2=6\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: First ball stops ($v_1=0$); second ball moves at $6\ \text{m/s}$.

examples.problem: A 3 kg body moving at 4 m/s collides with and sticks to a 1 kg body at rest (perfectly inelastic). Find the common velocity after the collision.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For a perfectly inelastic collision, momentum is conserved and the bodies move together: $v=\frac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute $m_1=3\ \text{kg}$, $u_1=4\ \text{m/s}$, $m_2=1\ \text{kg}$, $u_2=0$.
  3. Step 3: $v=\frac{3\times 4+1\times 0}{3+1}=\frac{12}{4}=3\ \text{m/s}$.

Answer: $v=3\ \text{m/s}$

examples.problem: In the perfectly inelastic collision of Example 4 (3 kg at 4 m/s sticking to 1 kg at rest, common velocity 3 m/s), find the kinetic energy lost.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Initial KE $=\frac{1}{2}m_1u_1^2+\frac{1}{2}m_2u_2^2=\frac{1}{2}\times 3\times 4^2+0=24\ \text{J}$.
  2. Step 2: Final KE $=\frac{1}{2}(m_1+m_2)v^2=\frac{1}{2}\times 4\times 3^2=18\ \text{J}$.
  3. Step 3: KE lost $=24-18=6\ \text{J}$ (converted to heat, sound and deformation).

Answer: KE lost $=6\ \text{J}$

examples.problem: A ball is dropped from a height of 5 m and rebounds to a height of 1.25 m. Find the coefficient of restitution between the ball and the floor.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Speed of approach $u=\sqrt{2gh_1}$ and speed of separation $v=\sqrt{2gh_2}$, so $e=\frac{v}{u}=\sqrt{\frac{h_2}{h_1}}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute $h_1=5\ \text{m}$, $h_2=1.25\ \text{m}$, giving $e=\sqrt{\frac{1.25}{5}}=\sqrt{0.25}$.
  3. Step 3: $e=0.5$.

Answer: $e=0.5$

recap: Power is the rate of doing work: $P=\frac{W}{t}$, measured in watts; $1\ \text{hp}=746\ \text{W}$.
In all collisions linear momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.
In a 1D elastic collision the relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation; equal masses exchange velocities.

quiz.q: The SI unit of power is the:
quiz.explanation: Power is work per unit time; $1\ \text{watt}=1\ \text{J/s}$.

quiz.q: Instantaneous power in terms of force and velocity is:
In a perfectly inelastic collision, which quantity is NOT conserved?
quiz.explanation: Momentum (and total energy) are conserved, but kinetic energy is not — the maximum possible KE is lost.

quiz.q: For a perfectly elastic collision, the coefficient of restitution is:
quiz.explanation: In a perfectly elastic collision the relative speeds of separation and approach are equal, so $e=1$.

online.title: Work, Energy and Power — Chapter Test

questions.q: Work done by a force is defined as:
questions.explanation: Work is the scalar (dot) product of force and displacement: $W=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}=Fs\cos\theta$.

questions.q: A force of 10 N moves a body 4 m at $60^\circ$ to the displacement. The work done is:
questions.explanation: $W=Fs\cos\theta=10\times 4\times\cos 60^\circ=40\times 0.5=20\ \text{J}$.

questions.q: The kinetic energy of a 2 kg body moving at 5 m/s is:
questions.explanation: $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\times 5^2=25\ \text{J}$.

questions.q: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done equals:
questions.explanation: $W_{net}=\Delta KE$ — the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

questions.q: For a variable force, work done equals the:
questions.explanation: $W=\int F\,dx$ is the area under the force-displacement graph.

questions.q: If the momentum of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
questions.explanation: $KE=\frac{p^2}{2m}\propto p^2$; doubling $p$ makes $KE$ four times larger.

questions.q: Gravitational potential energy of a body of mass $m$ at height $h$ is:
questions.explanation: Near the Earth's surface, $U=mgh$ relative to a chosen zero level.

questions.q: The potential energy stored in a spring of constant $k$ stretched by $x$ is:
questions.explanation: Spring PE is the area under $F=kx$, giving $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2$.

questions.q: Which of the following is a conservative force?
questions.explanation: Gravity does path-independent work and zero work over a closed loop, so it is conservative.

questions.q: A stone dropped from 20 m hits the ground at (take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$):
questions.explanation: By energy conservation $v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2\times 10\times 20}=\sqrt{400}=20\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.q: The SI unit of power is the:
questions.explanation: Power is work per unit time, measured in watts ($1\ \text{W}=1\ \text{J/s}$).

questions.q: Instantaneous power equals:
questions.explanation: $P=\frac{dW}{dt}=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}=Fv\cos\theta$.

questions.q: A pump raises 200 kg of water 10 m in 10 s. Its power is (take $g=10\ \text{m/s}^2$):
questions.explanation: $P=\frac{mgh}{t}=\frac{200\times 10\times 10}{10}=2000\ \text{W}$.

questions.q: In every collision the quantity always conserved is:
questions.explanation: Linear momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.

questions.q: When two equal masses collide elastically in 1D and one is initially at rest, they:
questions.explanation: For equal masses in an elastic collision, velocities are exchanged: the moving one stops and the other moves off.

questions.q: A 2 kg body at 3 m/s sticks to a 1 kg body at rest. The common velocity is:
questions.explanation: $v=\frac{2\times 3+1\times 0}{2+1}=\frac{6}{3}=2\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.q: The coefficient of restitution for a perfectly inelastic collision is:
questions.explanation: In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick, so the relative velocity of separation is zero, giving $e=0$.

imo.title: Work, Energy and Power — Olympiad Challenge

questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moves so that its position is $x=3t^2$ (x in metres, t in seconds). The work done by the net force in the first 2 s is:
questions.explanation: $v=\frac{dx}{dt}=6t$, so at $t=2$, $v=12\ \text{m/s}$, $u=0$. $W=\Delta KE=\frac{1}{2}m(12)^2=72m\ \text{J}$.

questions.q: A force $F=kx$ acts on a particle. The work done in moving it from $x=0$ to $x=a$ is:
questions.explanation: $W=\int_0^a kx\,dx=\frac{1}{2}ka^2$.

questions.q: Two bodies of equal mass moving with equal and opposite velocities $v$ undergo a perfectly inelastic head-on collision. The KE lost is:
questions.explanation: Total momentum is zero, so they stop; initial KE $=2\times\frac{1}{2}mv^2=mv^2$ is fully lost.

questions.q: A spring of constant $k$ is cut into two equal halves. The spring constant of each half is:
questions.explanation: Spring constant is inversely proportional to length; halving the length doubles $k$ to $2k$.

questions.q: A car of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$ is stopped in distance $d$ by braking. To stop the same car at speed $2v$ with the same retarding force, the distance needed is:
questions.explanation: $Fd=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $d\propto v^2$; doubling $v$ makes the distance $4d$.

questions.q: The power of a body moving with velocity $v$ under a constant force $F$ along its direction is:
questions.explanation: $P=\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}=Fv$ when force is along the velocity.

questions.q: A 1 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides elastically and head-on with a 3 kg ball at rest. The velocity of the 1 kg ball after collision is:
questions.explanation: $v_1=\frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1}{m_1+m_2}=\frac{(1-3)\times 4}{1+3}=\frac{-8}{4}=-2\ \text{m/s}$ (it bounces back).

questions.q: A particle moves under a force such that its KE is proportional to time, $KE\propto t$. Its speed is proportional to:
questions.explanation: $KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2\propto t$ gives $v^2\propto t$, so $v\propto\sqrt{t}$.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from height $h$ and the coefficient of restitution with the floor is $e$. The height after the first bounce is:
questions.explanation: Rebound speed is $e$ times the approach speed, so rebound height $=e^2h$ (height $\propto v^2$).

questions.q: An engine pumps water at a rate $\dot{m}$ (kg/s) giving it speed $v$. The power delivered to the water is:
questions.explanation: KE given per second $=\frac{1}{2}(\dot{m})v^2$, which is the power delivered.

questions.q: A block of mass 2 kg is pushed against a spring ($k=800\ \text{N/m}$) compressing it 0.1 m, then released on a frictionless floor. The block's speed when it leaves the spring is:
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{2}kx^2=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v=x\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=0.1\sqrt{\frac{800}{2}}=0.1\times 20=2\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.q: In a 1D elastic collision, the relative velocity of separation compared with the relative velocity of approach is:
questions.explanation: For a perfectly elastic collision, $u_1-u_2=v_2-v_1$ — the relative velocities of approach and separation are equal in magnitude.
